slides.headline: October 19, 1910: a boy was born in Lahore who would spend his career proving what crushes a dying star.
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar was born in Lahore, British India
slides.body: He moved to the US to pursue astrophysics, spending nearly six decades on the faculty at the University of Chicago until his death in 1995 - his uncle, C.V. Raman, had already won India's first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.

slides.headline: He showed that a white dwarf star's mass can't exceed about 1.44 times the Sun's - the 'Chandrasekhar limit.'
slides.body: His theoretical work on how stars are structured and how they evolve, developed decades earlier, won him the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with William A. Fowler.

slides.eyebrow: Why it matters for Viksit Bharat 2047
slides.headline: A Viksit Bharat needs theoretical scientists, not just engineers.
slides.body: Chandrasekhar's Nobel came from pure astrophysical theory - proof that Indian scientific talent could reshape fundamental physics itself, not only build applied technology.
